values.value: • Use your understanding of the decision process to guide the deal with confidence. • Confirm both the formal steps and the informal influence pattern. • Map approvals, procurement, finance, academic or L&D leadership, and user stakeholders. • Sequence your next actions to match how the customer actually decides. • Stay ahead of blockers instead of reacting late.
11|Strong
Buyer may say, 'The process is straightforward.' Response: 'Great. I will still map the key steps and owners so we keep the momentum and avoid surprises.'
Good. Use your process knowledge to plan the deal backward from approval, legal, and buying checkpoints.
Low risk. Turn process insight into close control.
Ask: 'Can we map the internal approval steps and owners so we do not lose time later?'
Strong

• Close the gaps before the deal reaches proposal or negotiation pressure. • Ask who signs, who recommends, who can delay, and who must be convinced. • Check whether procurement, finance, IT, academic council, or leadership approvals matter. • Turn the process into a visible deal map with owners and timing. • Better process clarity will make your next steps sharper.
11|Adequate
Buyer may say, 'More or less we know how this will move.' Response: 'That is a good start. I would like to tighten the last few process details so the forecast and proposal timing stay accurate.'
Tighten your understanding of the real decision path. Formal process alone is not enough; informal influence matters too.
Risk: Adequate process knowledge can still hide blockers.
Ask: 'Apart from the formal process, whose view really shapes the final decision here?'
Adequate

• Pause forward momentum long enough to understand how this deal really gets approved. • Do not rely on your contact's view alone. • Ask for the actual sign-off sequence and any unofficial influencers behind it. • Identify what stage the deal is truly in versus what it appears to be in. • You need process visibility before you push commercials further.
11|Weak
Buyer may say, 'We will figure the process out as we go.' Response: 'We can, but even a basic decision map now will save us from late-stage slippage.'
Stop guessing. Map all approvers, influencers, and hidden blockers before moving ahead.
High risk: Weak decision-map control.
Ask: 'Who signs, who influences, and who can quietly slow this down if not aligned?'
Weak

• You are effectively flying blind on how the customer will decide. • Find out who recommends, who approves, who vetoes, and what steps must happen in between. • Ask whether there are committee reviews, procurement gates, budget approvals, or academic governance steps. • Without this, forecasting and proposal timing will be unreliable. • Treat this as a priority discovery gap.
11|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'Let us focus on the solution first.' Response: 'Happy to. I also want to understand how the decision will actually happen so I can support you properly at each step.'
Do not confuse activity with progress. First learn how this account really decides and who carries weight.
High risk: No decision-process clarity.
Ask: 'Can you help me understand how decisions like this usually get made internally?'
Don't know
How is our understanding of the formal and the informal decision making process?
